findings.summary: The "~1000x cheaper to start than a thread" claim contradicts the creation costs given in the table directly above it.
findings.evidence: Table: Create — Goroutine "~1–2 µs", OS thread "~10–100 µs". Bullet: "~1000x cheaper to start than a thread." 1–2 µs vs 10–100 µs is 5–100x, not 1000x.
findings.fix: Either fix the ratio to match the table ("~10–50x cheaper to start") or fix the table row to real measured goroutine-spawn cost (~0.2–0.5 µs, giving ~20–100x). Also reconcile the caption's "costs 2 KB and about a microsecond" with whichever number you keep. If you want a 1000x figure, attach it to memory (2 KB vs 8 MB), where it actually holds.

findings.summary: "`len(allp) == GOMAXPROCS`, fixed at startup" is wrong — GOMAXPROCS is mutable at runtime, as the very next bullet and the Go 1.25 callout both say.
findings.evidence: "`len(allp) == GOMAXPROCS`, fixed at startup." immediately followed by "Change with `runtime.GOMAXPROCS(n)`." and the callout "Go 1.25: cgroup-aware — `GOMAXPROCS` now reads the container CPU quota"; the Go 1.25 notes add that "the runtime periodically updates GOMAXPROCS if the number of logical CPUs available or the cgroup CPU bandwidth limit change."
findings.fix: Change to "`len(allp) == GOMAXPROCS`, resized by `procresize` (stop-the-world)." and add to the 1.25 callout that the runtime now re-reads the quota periodically unless GOMAXPROCS was set manually via the env var or `runtime.GOMAXPROCS`.

findings.summary: `runtime.SetMaxThreads` does not exist — the function is `runtime/debug.SetMaxThreads`.
findings.evidence: "`runtime.SetMaxThreads` defaults to 10,000." The `runtime` package exposes no `SetMaxThreads`; `runtime/debug` documents "SetMaxThreads sets the maximum number of operating system threads that the Go program can use... The initial setting is 10,000 threads."
findings.fix: Change the bullet to "`runtime/debug.SetMaxThreads` defaults to 10,000." (The sibling `debug.SetMaxStack` on page 7 is already correctly attributed.)

findings.summary: The syscall handoff bullets claim the P is detached and rehomed immediately, which contradicts the actual `_Psyscall`/`retake` mechanism the handbook describes correctly two pages later.
findings.evidence: Page 3: "Handoff: M blocks in a syscall, its P is detached. / P is handed to another M immediately. / A blocked thread never idles a core." Page 5: "`entersyscall` marks the P `_Psyscall`. / Returns fast: the M reacquires the same P, nothing happens. / Runs long: `sysmon` calls `retake`, hands the P to another M."
findings.fix: Replace the two bullets with the page-5-accurate version: "M enters a syscall → its P goes to `_Psyscall`, still attached. / Short syscall: the same M takes the P back. / Long syscall (or queued work): `sysmon`/`entersyscallblock` calls `handoffp`, another M picks it up." Soften "never idles a core" to "a core is idled only for the retake delay."

findings.summary: The "Run Queues" cell diagram clips and overflows its box labels so the slot names are unreadable.
findings.evidence: Leftmost cell reads "runn" cut off at the cell border instead of "runnext"; the final label "global" spills outside its box outline, and the index row "0 1 2 3 4 5 6" does not line up with the seven drawn cells.
findings.fix: Widen the cells (or shrink the label font / abbreviate to fit) in the Run Queues figure so "runnext" and "global" render fully inside their boxes, and align the 0-6 index ticks with the cell centres.

findings.summary: Page 4 ends with a bullet block about cooperative and async preemption, a full page before preemption is introduced on page 5.
findings.evidence: Page 4 final block: "Cooperative gap: tight loop, no calls, no allocation = never yields.", "Async preemption needed a compiler change, not just a runtime one.", "Register maps at every instruction is the price paid." — the terms are first defined on page 5 in the cards diagram ("Cooperative (all)": "Prologue checks SP vs `stackguard0`" / "Async (1.14+)": "`SIGURG` to the thread"). It also wedges itself between page 4's `GODEBUG=schedtrace=1000` code block and page 5's opening table that decodes that command's fields ("`runqueue=`","global queue depth").
findings.fix: Move that four-bullet block to page 5, directly after the "Two Preemptions" cards diagram, so the schedtrace code block on page 4 runs straight into the schedtrace field table on page 5.

findings.summary: The "A Channel Is hchan" field diagram clips and overruns its cell labels.
findings.evidence: Cell labels read "buf" / "ring" wrapped across the cell border, "coun" clipped instead of "count", and "sendq" / "recvq" cross the vertical dividers and run past the right edge of the last cell.
findings.fix: Enlarge the hchan figure's cell widths or reduce the label font so "buf ring", "elemsize", "count", "lock", "sendq", "recvq" each fit on one line inside their own cell.

findings.summary: Page 7 closes with a `select` example that turns a case off by nilling its channel, but `select` semantics and nil-channel blocking are only taught on page 8.
findings.evidence: Page 7 last block: "for { select {", "case v := <-in: use(v)", "case <-done: in = nil  // disable case". The explanation arrives on page 8: "op on nil chan","blocks forever" and the callout "nil is a feature — Blocking forever is deliberately useful: set a `select` case's channel to nil to switch that case off for good."
findings.fix: Move this code block to page 8 immediately after the "nil is a feature" callout, and end page 7 with the `hchan` array diagram as the bridge into the channels page.

findings.summary: The `time.After` leak claim is obsolete: since Go 1.23 the garbage collector reclaims unreferenced, unstopped timers, so `time.After` in a select loop is no longer a leak.
findings.evidence: "`time.After` allocates a timer not collected until it fires." / "In a hot `select` loop that is a real leak — see the leaks page." / "Use `time.NewTimer` + `Stop`, or `context.WithTimeout`." — but the current `time.After` docs state: "Before Go 1.23, this documentation warned that the underlying Timer would not be recovered by the garbage collector until the timer fired... As of Go 1.23, the garbage collector can recover unreferenced, unstopped timers," and "there is no reason to prefer NewTimer when After will do."
findings.fix: Rewrite as a version-scoped note: "`time.After` leaked a timer until it fired — pre-1.23 only. Go 1.23+ GCs unreferenced timers, so `time.After` in a select loop is fine (needs `go >= 1.23` in go.mod). The remaining cost is one allocation per iteration." Drop the "real leak" bullet and demote the `NewTimer`+`Stop` line to an allocation-avoidance tip.

findings.summary: The semaphore pattern's code sits at the end of page 8 while its explanatory bullets appear on page 9 after the worker pool, unheaded, so they read as part of the worker pool.
findings.evidence: Page 8 ends with heading "Semaphore" plus "sem := make(chan struct{}, N)" / "sem <- struct{}{}          // acquire". Page 9 then runs "Worker Pool" code and bullets ("N goroutines ranging over one jobs channel.") and only afterwards an unheaded block: "A buffered channel of size N is the whole implementation.", "Different goal than a pool: one goroutine per item still."
findings.fix: Keep the worker pool first, then place a "Semaphore" heading with the `sem := make(chan struct{}, N)` code and the four buffered-channel bullets together on page 9; drop the orphan heading and code from page 8.

findings.summary: The caption promises two payoffs — a goroutine-leak taxonomy and a pprof debugging workflow — that no title in the ten-page deck names.
findings.evidence: Caption: "the nine ways goroutines leak, and the pprof ladder for finding them. Save it for the next time RSS climbs while your heap stays flat." Titles list ends with "Patterns That Hold Up in Production" and "Ownership, Context, and Clean Shutdown"; no title mentions leaks, pprof, or diagnosis.
findings.fix: If pages 9–10 do cover the leak taxonomy and pprof, retitle them to say so (e.g. "The Nine Ways Goroutines Leak" and "Finding Leaks: The pprof Ladder"); if they don't, cut those clauses from the caption and promise what the deck actually delivers (production patterns, ownership, clean shutdown).

findings.summary: The loop-variable snippet uses range-over-int, which itself requires Go 1.22, so the "pre-1.22 printed 3,3,3" comment describes behaviour this code could never have had.
findings.evidence: "for i := range 3 {" ... "}  // pre-1.22 printed 3,3,3" — ranging over an integer was added in Go 1.22, the same release as the per-iteration loop variable; pre-1.22 this program does not compile.
findings.fix: Use the classic three-clause form so the comment is true: `for i := 0; i < 3; i++ { go func(){ fmt.Println(i) }() }  // pre-1.22: usually 3,3,3`. Optionally note that the 1.22 loopvar semantics apply only when the main module's go.mod declares `go 1.22` or later.

findings.summary: Page 1 uses `P` as a known entity in the free-list bullets, but `P` is only defined on page 2.
findings.evidence: Page 1: "Dead `g`s go on a per-P free list (`gFree`) and recycle." and the takeaway "Spawn-and-die churn reuses `g` structs off `gFree`". Page 2 first defines it: "`P`","processor","permit + queue".
findings.fix: On page 1 say "a per-processor free list (`gFree`) — see the G/M/P page" or drop the `P` qualifier entirely ("dead `g`s go on a free list and are recycled"), leaving the per-P detail for page 3's "Why P Exists At All" section.

findings.summary: Connector lines in the scheduler flow diagram run through the middle of the node boxes instead of terminating at their edges.
findings.evidence: A horizontal line crosses straight through the "runnext" box label, and lines pass over the "mcache" and "g0 stack" boxes in the lower rows of the scheduler diagram.
findings.fix: Route the scheduler diagram's edges to stop at node borders (or increase vertical spacing between the P/M/G row and the runq/runnext/mcache row) so no connector overlaps box text.

findings.summary: The page titled "The M:N Model — G, M, and P" never introduces M:N or G/M/P; both were already taught on page 2, so the title sends a learner to the wrong page.
findings.evidence: Page 2 carries "Three Letters" with the table rows "`G`","goroutine","the work" … and "M:N = M goroutines multiplexed onto N OS threads."; page 3 opens with "Threads Are Separate" and covers run queues and `g0` only.
findings.fix: Retitle page 2 to "The M:N Model — G, M, and P" (folding the lifecycle/GOMAXPROCS bullets under it) and retitle page 3 to what it actually teaches, e.g. "Run Queues, Threads, and `g0`".

findings.summary: The `scheddetail` command line is inert as written — `scheddetail=1` produces no output unless `schedtrace` is also set.
findings.evidence: "GODEBUG=scheddetail=1 ./app    # + per G/M/P" — the runtime GODEBUG docs say "setting schedtrace=X **and** scheddetail=1 causes the scheduler to emit detailed multiline info every X milliseconds."
findings.fix: Change the second line to `GODEBUG=schedtrace=1000,scheddetail=1 ./app  # + per G/M/P`.

findings.summary: "Newly readied Gs skip the thread wake-up" states as a general rule the opposite of the `wakep()` invariant listed two lines later.
findings.evidence: "Newly readied Gs skip the thread wake-up (~tens of µs saved)." vs "Invariant: work submitted while an idle P exists must call `wakep()`." Readying a G calls `wakep` unless a spinning M is already hunting; the wake-up is skipped only in that case.
findings.fix: Reword to attribute the saving to the spinning M: "If an M is already spinning, readying a G needs no thread wake-up — that is what the spin buys. Otherwise `wakep()` runs."

findings.summary: The `findRunnable()` lookup order names the netpoller and epoll as sources before either is explained on page 6.
findings.evidence: Page 4 flow diagram nodes "netpoller" and table row "4","netpoller","epoll check", with no gloss; page 6 first defines it: "Network reads and writes park the goroutine, not the thread." and the OS table "Linux","`epoll`".
findings.fix: Add a one-line gloss in the page 4 table's Cost column or a bullet — e.g. "netpoller = ready network I/O, detailed later" — so step 4 is not an unexplained name.

findings.summary: The `LockOSThread` code example ends page 5 but its explanation only comes on page 6, after the netpoller and cgo material.
findings.evidence: Page 5 last block: "runtime.LockOSThread()", "defer runtime.UnlockOSThread()". Page 6 explains it several blocks later: "`LockOSThread` pins a goroutine to its M.", "Always pair with `UnlockOSThread` in a `defer`." — after "The Netpoller" table and the "Three M-hogs" sidebox.
findings.fix: Move the `LockOSThread` code to page 6 so it sits directly above the four `LockOSThread` bullets, and end page 5 on the syscall-jitter takeaway.

findings.summary: Page 6 ends with the stack-overflow fatal error output before the 1 GB limit and its unrecoverability are taught on page 7.
findings.evidence: Page 6 last block: "runtime: goroutine stack exceeds", "  1000000000-byte limit", "fatal error: stack overflow" — with no preceding mention of a limit; page 7 then introduces "Hard Limits" ("64-bit","1 GB") and the sidebox "Unrecoverable".
findings.fix: Move the error output to page 7 directly under the "Hard Limits" table and the "Unrecoverable" sidebox.

findings.summary: Skipping `cancel()` on a standard `WithCancel`/`WithTimeout` does not leak a goroutine — no goroutine is spawned in the common case.
findings.evidence: "Skipping it leaks the timer and goroutine until the parent dies." `context.WithCancel` registers the child in the parent's child set; `propagateCancel` only starts a watchdog goroutine when the parent is a non-standard `Context` implementation, and `WithTimeout`'s timer is released when the deadline fires.
findings.fix: Reword to "Skipping it pins the child context (and, for `WithTimeout`, its timer) in the parent's child set until the parent is cancelled — plus any goroutine still selecting on `ctx.Done()`."
